title: US White House Allegedly Traded 'Abduction Rights' for UFO Technology in 1954, Podcast Claims
excerpt: Investigative journalist Ross Coulthart examines claims of a secret 1954 UFO retrieval programme authorised by the White House, highlighting disputed documents and whistleblower accounts.
content:
Investigative journalist Ross Coulthart has detailed allegations claiming the White House authorised a secret UFO retrieval programme in 1954 that exchanged advanced non-human technology for human abduction rights, during an episode of his Reality Check podcast.

The narrative centres on supposed clandestine meetings between President Dwight D. Eisenhower's administration and non-human intelligences

However, an analysis of primary records indicates that these claims rely on disputed documents, long-standing UFO folklore, and unverified whistleblower accounts rather than authenticated government history.

Disputed Documents and the Eisenhower Allegations

The foundational lore surrounding these claims draws heavily on accounts of a supposed February 1954 summit involving President Eisenhower at Edwards Air Force Base in California, an event conventional historical records identify as a routine trip during which the president received emergency dental treatment.

Alternative versions within UFO literature relocate the alleged encounter to Holloman Air Force Base in New Mexico. Over the decades, these storylines have been referred to by some UFO researchers as the 'Eisenhower alien treaty,' though no official documentation or historical evidence supports the existence of any such accord.

Much of the modern narrative is entangled with the controversial 'Majestic-12' (MJ-12) papers. In December 1984, UFO researcher Jaime Shandera received an anonymous package containing undeveloped 35mm film.

When developed, the film revealed what purported to be classified briefing documents dated November 1952, outlining a high-level committee established by President Harry S. Truman in 1947 to manage recovered extraterrestrial craft.

However, official government investigations quickly debunked the material. The Federal Bureau of Investigation's publicly released records show that a subsequent Air Force investigation determined the documents were fake, leading the FBI to officially mark the file with a 'BOGUS' designation.

Whistleblower Claims and Official Pentagon Denials

Coulthart linked these historical allegations to recent claims made by former intelligence official David Grusch concerning a decades-long, covert US government programme dedicated to retrieving and reverse-engineering non-human craft. Grusch filed a formal whistleblower complaint with the Intelligence Community Inspector General in 2022 and subsequently testified under oath before a US House Oversight Committee panel in July 2023.

While congressional lawmakers noted that the Inspector General deemed Grusch's complaint 'credible and urgent,' those official procedural findings applied strictly to the handling of whistleblower reporting rights and did not validate his underlying claims regarding extraterrestrial technology.

Directly countering such claims, the US Department of Defence's All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office (AARO) released its comprehensive Historical Record Report in 2024. AARO concluded that thorough investigations found no evidence that any Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena (UAP) represented off-world technology, nor any evidence confirming the existence of classified reverse-engineering programmes.

As of September 2026, no publicly released physical evidence or official verification supports allegations of recovered non-human craft or agreements with extraterrestrial entities.

Strategic Speculation and Cold War Disinformation

Addressing the geopolitical dimensions of the claims, Coulthart speculated that if any nation were to acquire technology capable of instantaneous global movement, it would render traditional nuclear deterrence and the doctrine of Mutual Assured Destruction obsolete.

He argued that such immense strategic stakes could explain why major military powers, including the United States, Russia, and China, maintain rigorous secrecy surrounding UAP research, though there is no confirmed evidence that foreign powers possess recovered non-human hardware.

Coulthart referenced an unverified account from a viewer claiming personal contact with non-human entities, while acknowledging that the statement lacked sufficient corroboration to be substantiated. Historians note that claims of this nature emerged against a backdrop of active Cold War counterintelligence operations.

During the 1980s, elements within the US military, including former Air Force Office of Special Investigations (AFOSI) agent Richard Doty, engaged in documented disinformation efforts targeted at UFO researchers. Notably, researcher Bill Moore admitted in a 1989 address that he had cooperated with government contacts to spread deceptive material within the research community, further obscuring the boundary between authentic classification and deliberate deception.

Consequently, editorial standards require treating these extraordinary assertions with strict caution.
